newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's Belka vows to shield budget from politics.
newsitem.headline: Poland's Belka vows to shield budget from politics.

text.p: Polish Finance Minister Marek Belka, working on a 1998 budget draft that aims to slash the deficit, vowed on Friday to resist any pressure from parties campaigning for parliamentary elections on September 21.

Belka, a non-party economist, rejected calls by the co-ruling Peasant Party (PSL) to drop his plan to slash the budget deficit next year, saying the group was preparing the ground for demanding higher spending on agriculture.

He said he would continue working on the draft assuming that the budget gap would be cut to 1.9 percent of gross domestic product next year from the 2.8 percent planned for 1997, a measure necessary to cool domestic demand and control the trade deficit.
"We are in the midst of the election campaign. If I took notice of politicians' demands we would land on the moon and not with a sensible budget," Belka told a news conference.
"I am in charge of the budget and I see no possiblity of increasing the deficit beyond...1.9 percent," he added.
Belka suggested that Friday's calls by the Peasant Party to let the gap stay at the 1997 level of 2.8 percent of GDP was likely to translate subsequently into demands for higher farm spending.
"I think the PSL is preparing grounds for changing priorities in the budget," he said, adding that education and security would continue to be his budget priorities.
Belka earlier said that a higher budget deficit would continue to fuel strong demand for imported goods and might push the swelling trade and current account deficits out of control.

The central bank says that if the current account deficit -- forecast to grow to $6 billion this year from $1.35 billion in 1996 -- expands too much in 1998, Poland might eventually have to devalue the zloty.
The bank says this would boost inflation and undermine economic growth.

It advocates balancing the budget next year or at least cutting the deficit to 1.5 percent of GDP before getting rid of it in 1999. This measure would help Poland to avoid a Czech-style financial crisis, the bank says.
The Czech Republic has had to devalue its currency and take strict measures to curb imports after its foreign trade deficit ballooned and industrial output shrank.

But Belka said he was confident that the central bank's strict monetary policy coupled with a deficit cut would be enough to contain the growing trade deficit. "I have more confidence in the central bank's monetary policy," he said.
PSL agrees that the trade deficit growth had to be curbed but said this should involve stimulating exports rather than limiting imports by cooling internal demand.

Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz, a member of the dominant ex-communist party in the coalition, backs Belka's austerity plans and his political allies in the government can overrule the Peasants' objections during cabinet votes.
Belka wants to finish his budget draft by early September so the government can submit it shortly after the elections.
Under his proposal, next year's budgetary spending will be 142.9 billion zlotys ($43.4 billion), with revenues of 133.3 billion zlotys and the deficit at 9.6 billion zlotys ($2.9 billion).
Inflation is to fall to 9.5 percent in December next year from 14.6 percent in May, while economic growth is forecast to continue at this year's rate of 5.5 percent.
